content: The diversity of infectious agents necessitates collaboration among stakeholders working at the animal-human interface, presenting a unique challenge in setting priorities for research and intervention. This report specifically addresses the following infections: 1. Helminth Infections: Taeniasis/Cysticercosis Echinococcosis Zoonotic Schistosomiasis Foodborne Trematodiases 2. Protozoan Infections: Toxoplasmosis Cryptosporidiosis 3. Bacterial Infections: Brucellosis Enteric Infections Bovine Tuberculosis Anthrax 4. Viral Infections: Rabies Rotavirus infection was excluded from this report as it is already receiving significant attention globally, with effective vaccines available and expected to be widely deployed in the near future. Diarrheal diseases, which are closely linked to poverty due to limited access to safe water, sanitation, and healthcare, are also considered in this report. These diseases are particularly relevant as they enhance the cost-effectiveness of ecosystem, water supply, and sanitation improvements, which can reduce the burden of diarrheal and other infectious agents, whether zoonotic or not. The Disease Reference Group on Zoonoses and Marginalized Infectious Diseases of Poverty (DRG 6) was composed of 13 experts in zoonotic diseases and cross-cutting themes. Members were selected from research institutions, international organizations, health and medical organizations, and governmental bodies worldwide. Geographic distribution and gender balance were considered to ensure input from disease-endemic countries and regions. Members were formally appointed for an initial two-year term and were required to declare any conflicts of interest and confidentiality. The DRG was hosted in the WHO Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean (EMRO) in Cairo, Egypt, to ensure that countries most affected by poverty-related diseases contributed to and shared ownership of the research agenda. The think tank included researchers and public health experts from the most affected countries, with support from WHO country and regional offices. A preliminary informal consultation was held in Geneva in June 2009 to discuss the scope and framework of the DRG. This was necessary as TDR had not previously been involved in these diseases, despite their significant impact on the poor in endemic countries. The DRG was established to systematically review research evidence, assess control challenges, highlight scientific advances, and provide guidance on priority areas and research gaps. The prioritization process involved informal consultations, semi-quantitative prioritization exercises, stakeholder consultations, and the development of matrices based on specific indicators. The DRG also utilized authoritative reports and peer-reviewed publications to identify research priorities. A semi-quantitative approach allowed for a multidimensional analysis of diseases, cross-cutting topics, and interventions, with priorities rated on a scale of 1 to 5. Stakeholder consultations were integral to the process, ensuring validation, endorsement, and uptake of research priorities. These consultations included representatives from ministries of health, agriculture, and animal resources in endemic countries, as well as international organizations and academic institutions. The consultations emphasized the importance of research at the human-animal interface and provided input on real needs in affected countries. The DRG's findings and priorities were summarized in a report, which underwent external and internal reviews before being published as an Expert Report in the WHO Technical Report Series. The report highlighted the burden of disease, defined as the size of a health problem measured by cost, mortality, morbidity, or other indicators. Various methods for estimating disease burden in humans and animals were summarized, including mortality rates, disease-specific incidence and prevalence, quality-adjusted life years (QALYs), and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs). The report emphasized the need for special studies to address gaps in data quality and availability, particularly for diseases with significant sequelae. It also highlighted the importance of understanding the natural history of diseases and their sequelae to improve burden estimates and inform control strategies.
